## The mean is nonlinear in the parameters {visibility="hidden"}

$$
\mu = f(x, \theta),
$$

and $f$ is not a straight line in $\theta$. A Michaelis–Menten curve, $\mu = \theta_1 x / (\theta_2 + x)$, is the usual example. $\theta_2$ is not a slope.

::: {.notes}
Hidden from the audience deck. Use it only if someone asks how a named curve differs from a GLM and from a smooth. One minute.
:::

## A GLM is linear on the link {visibility="hidden"}

$$
g(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$

The mean can be a curve in $x$. The parameters still enter as a sum. That is the difference from $f(x, \theta)$ above: nonlinearity in $\mu$ is not nonlinearity in $\theta$.

::: {.notes}
Draw $g$ as the straight step and $f$ as the curved step. Do not open `nls` unless they have a named $f$.
:::

## A smooth does not name $f$ {visibility="hidden"}

A smoother estimates a curve $f(x)$ from the data. Nonlinear least squares requires the formula first, then estimates $\theta$.

- Wrong $f$: the fit can look close and $\hat\theta$ still answers the wrong question
- The start matters: the criterion can have more than one valley
- The errors are still an assumption, usually additive on the scale of $Y$

::: {.notes}
Three bullets only. The smooth section is the unnamed curve. This slide is the named one. Keep it hidden unless asked.
:::
